title: Information revelation in the futures market: Evidence from single stock futures
abstract: Abstract This paper analyzes 31 months of data on 137 single‐stock futures (SSFs) traded on OneChicago. The results indicate that on the days they trade, SSFs contribute approximately 24% of the price discovery for underlying stocks. Information revelation in the SSFs market decreases with the ratio of spreads in the futures and the stock markets and the volatility in the stock market. Moreover, the quality of the market for the underlying stocks improves substantially after the introduction of the SSFs market, with the largest improvement occurring on days with SSFs trading. © 2008 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. Jrl Fut Mark 28:335– 353, 2008

summary.oneLiner: Single stock futures on OneChicago contributed about 24 percent of price discovery for underlying US stocks, and underlying stock market quality improved after their launch.
summary.overview: This paper asks whether trading in single stock futures, contracts on individual shares, helps set the prices of the underlying stocks. Using 31 months of OneChicago data on 137 stocks, the authors estimate that futures account for about 24 percent of price discovery, which they describe as a significant share. The futures market's share rises when futures volume is high relative to stock volume and when futures spreads are low relative to stock spreads. Underlying stocks also showed lower spreads and lower adverse selection costs after futures listings, and the authors report evidence of both market-wide and stock-specific learning over time.
summary.question: Do single stock futures contribute to price discovery (the process by which trading reveals information in prices) for their underlying stocks, and how does futures trading affect stock market quality?
summary.method: The authors apply the Hasbrouck (1995) information share methodology to estimate each market's contribution to price discovery, adapting it to futures prices using a no-arbitrage model. They then run cross-sectional, Fama-MacBeth style monthly, and pooled panel regressions to explain information share, and compare stock market liquidity before and after futures listings and on trade versus no-trade days. They also test calendar-time and listing-event-time trends to look for learning.
summary.data: Daily and intraday data from January 2003 to July 2005 for 137 NYSE and NASDAQ stocks with single stock futures on the OneChicago exchange. Stock quote and trade data come from the NYSE TAQ database and futures data from OneChicago. Only the shortest maturity contract per stock is used, and the sample is restricted to days with at least three trades and two price changes.
findings: Single stock futures contribute approximately 24 percent of information revelation (price discovery) for underlying stocks; lower and upper bound averages are 24.4 and 24.6 percent, significantly different from zero.

The futures information share increases with the futures-to-stock volume ratio and decreases with the futures-to-stock spread ratio and with stock volatility; the authors note the volatility sign was an empirical question.
The information share does not appear to depend on whether the underlying stock is listed on NYSE or NASDAQ.
After futures listings, the underlying stock's quoted spread fell 20.2 percent and effective spread fell 18.6 percent; the adverse selection component (lambda) fell from 12.3 to 10.2 percent.
Stock market quality is better on days with futures trading than on days without, which the authors say is consistent with informed traders moving to the futures market.

Evidence suggests both market-level and security-level learning, associated with greater efficiency over time, though the listing-time information share trend is only marginally significant at the 10 percent level.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors state that the futures market plays an important role in price discovery for underlying stocks and that a liquid futures market makes a significant contribution to price discovery. They suggest informed traders may find futures a lower-cost venue than options, and that the futures market may act as a venue for informed trading. The findings are associated with, rather than proven to cause, improved stock market quality.
